title: Chimichanga
subtitle: A deep-fried beef burrito, crispy outside and molten inside
excerpt: A flour tortilla filled with spiced beef, rice, and beans, then deep-fried until golden and shatteringly crisp. Served with soured cream, guacamole, and salsa.
sourceNotes: Chimichanga: the deep-fried burrito is claimed by both Tucson, Arizona (El Charro Café) and Phoenix, Arizona (Macayo's Mexican Kitchen) as an accidental invention of the mid-20th century. The Tucson origin story is most widely cited. Drawn from classic American Tex-Mex and Arizona-Mexican cooking sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Best made fresh. The fried shell goes soft on refrigerating and doesn't reheat well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The beef filling can be made a day ahead. Fry the chimichangas just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A deep-fried burrito originating in Arizona, made by filling a large flour tortilla and sealing it before frying to produce a crispy, golden shell around the cooked filling.

content.text: is a burrito that has been deep-fried: the flour tortilla seals the filling inside a crisp, golden shell while the beef and cheese inside melt together. The frying takes 3-4 minutes per batch. Oil temperature matters; at 180°C, the shell crisps without absorbing excess oil.

items.prepNote: drained and rinsed, half a tin
large flour tortillas, at least 30 cm
mashed with lime juice and salt

content.text: A large, deep frying pan holds enough oil to fry one or two chimichangas at a time. The seam must be sealed and placed into the oil first so it fuses before the chimichanga can open up.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a frying pan. Cook {{onion}} finely chopped onion for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic for 1 minute. Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince; cook 5-6 minutes until browned. Stir in the chilli powder, cumin, and smoked paprika. Season with salt. Stir in the drained black beans. The filling should be dry, not saucy; drain excess fat if needed. Cool slightly before filling.

Warm each flour tortilla in a dry pan. Place 4-5 tablespoons of beef filling and a quarter of the cheese in the lower third. Fold the bottom up, fold in the sides tightly, then roll up to form a sealed parcel. Press the seam firmly to close it.
Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of vegetable oil in a deep, wide frying pan to 180°C. Test with a cube of bread; it should turn golden in 30 seconds.

Lower each chimichanga seam-side down into the hot oil. Fry for 1.5-2 minutes until the underside is golden and the seam has sealed. Turn carefully and fry the other sides for 1-1.5 minutes each until golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper. Fry in batches so the oil temperature doesn't drop.
Serve immediately with soured cream, mashed avocado, and lime wedges.

items.symptom: Chimichanga bursts open in the oil
items.cause: Seam not properly sealed, or too much filling
items.fix: The seam must be pressed firmly and placed seam-side down into the oil first; the heat seals it in place within 30 seconds. Use no more than 5 tablespoons of filling.

items.symptom: Shell is pale and greasy rather than golden
items.fix: Wait until the oil reaches 180°C before adding the chimichangas. Adding them too soon soaks the tortilla with oil instead of crisping it.

items.symptom: Filling is still cold inside when the shell is golden
items.fix: Use the filling while still warm; it heats through in the 3-4 minutes of frying. Cold filling from the fridge won't heat through in time.

items.cause: Filling too dry and bulky, creating pressure points
items.fix: Keep the filling slightly moist and avoid overpacking. A dry filling packs too dense and tears the tortilla from the inside.

content.text: The chimichanga is claimed by Arizona, most famously by El Charro Café in Tucson, where the story goes that a burrito was dropped into the deep fryer by accident and emerged golden rather than ruined. Whether or not the story is true, the chimichanga became a mainstay of Arizona-Mexican and Tex-Mex menus by the 1970s. It's a dish that requires some confidence at the fryer but rewards the effort.
